statement.p:
In this activity, we will look at some examples of matrix transformations.
To begin, suppose that A is the matrix A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right].
with associated matrix transformation T(\xvec) = A\xvec.
What is T\left(\twovec{1}{-2}\right)?
What is T\left(\twovec{1}{0}\right)?
What is T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right)?
Is there a vector \xvec such that T(\xvec) = \twovec{3}{0}?
Write T\left(\twovec xy\right) as a two-dimensional vector.
Suppose that T(\xvec) = A\xvec where
A=\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp -3 \\ -2 \amp 1 \amp 4 \amp -4 \end{array}\right] .
What is the dimension of the vectors \xvec that are inputs for T?
What is the dimension of the vectors T(\xvec)=A\xvec that are outputs?
If we describe this transformation as T:\real^n\to\real^m, what are the values of n and m and how do they relate to the shape of A?
Describe the vectors \xvec for which T(\xvec) = \zerovec.
If A is the matrix A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} \vvec_1 \amp \vvec_2 \end{array}\right], what is T\left(\twovec10\right) in terms of the vectors \vvec_1 and \vvec_2? What about T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right)?
Suppose that A is a 3\times 2 matrix and that T(\xvec)=A\xvec. If
T\left(\twovec{1}{0}\right) = \threevec{3}{-1}{1}, T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right) = \threevec{2}{2}{-1} , what is the matrix A?

li.p:
If A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp 2 \end{array}\right], then
T\left(\twovec{1}{-2}\right) = A\twovec{1}{-2} = \twovec{0}{-3}.
T\left(\twovec{1}{0}\right) = A\twovec{1}{0} = \twovec{2}{1}.
T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right) = A\twovec{0}{1} = \twovec{1}{2}.
T\left(\twovec xy\right) = \twovec{2x+y}{x+2y}.
We seek a vector \xvec such that T(\xvec) = A\xvec=\twovec{3}{0}. We can solve this equation to find the unique solution \xvec=\twovec{2}{-1}.

Now if
A=\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 3 \amp 3 \amp -2 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 1 \amp -3 \\ -2 \amp 1 \amp 4 \amp -4 \end{array}\right]\text{,}
the matrix has dimensions 3\times4.
\xvec must be a four-dimensional vector.
A\xvec must be a three-dimensional vector.
For this matrix, we have T:\real^4\to\real^3. In general, if A is an m\times n matrix, T:\real^n\to\real^m.
If we solve the homogeneous equation A\xvec=\zerovec, we find that \xvec=x_4\fourvec{-3}{2}{-1}{1}.
T\left(\twovec{1}{0}\right) = \vvec_1, the first column of the matrix. Similarly, T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right) gives the second column of the matrix.
